RAMHDAD, March 20 (Reuters) - Syrian officials on Monday said two bomb blasts that were possibly fired by militants and weapons led by members of the Islamic group, killing at least one nine people in one Syrian town, according to a source overseeing the attack.

State security spokesman Bahram Kamal told Reuters News on Monday the blasts had been fired from a location near Maham town in Qaabira province, adding no more details.

“The bombs that were fired were aimed by militant weapons led by members of the Jaaz State group (IS), which has been accused of carrying terrorism in Iraq and Syria and is Iran’s close ally with Iran,” the source said.

Syria’s foreign security spokesman Husaf Al-Assdar Zranan told Syrian news agency APA that IS had no explicit responsibility for the blasts.

“The bombs were fired from a different direction, suggesting they were set off at a site located about 20 kilometers away. No other shots have been recorded from the site,” Zranan said.

At least one civilian person was injured in the attack. A Syrian news agency said another man was also injured from being hit by a nearby car, while another person was injured from air damage on the car’s roof. The government did not provide further details.

The UN said at least 23 people had also been killed in the attack as opposition groups claim IS holds control of the Syrian state.

The series of bomb attacks have sparked a growing tension on the front of the Afghan war and an worsening social divisions in both parts of Syria.

Worries for some peace in the conflict have risen to Damascus, where Damascus and Tehran have tried to repair their differences with their Islamic groups.

Then there is a rising pace for machines that can talk to people, control crimes, and maybe even automaticallyize autonomous vehicles. A team of Columbia University and Harvard University and Brown Mellon University researchers are beginning work on a camera that can sense the velocity of infrared beams and capture digital images from distance in ways that would feel like sitting on a bench. Researchers expect it to arrive in about 200 years, but field testing is expected to take place by the end of this year. What are you waiting?

Some universities have also been putting their sights on developing computer systems that can help researchers collect and compare large amounts of data that would need to answer questions similar to search systems. Whatever in their niche, the projects on their way will likely extend to just about every sphere of human life.

As these projects move forward, the coming years will also encourage a group of scientists to think carefully about the future of extremely intelligent technology and how its impact on our society. One example for such thought, says Michael Wwerhwek, an assistant professor of computer engineering at the University of Washington, and a co-author who wrote on this study in today’s paper in Nature Science.

“For example, we could see the future of new devices that use these data as smart tools and provide ways that people have access to very complex and important data, whether in the context of what a person looks like, or even in the context of income, work, health, and income,” Wether says. “So what else will these devices have to do with that data?”

Keep in mind, for one, is that the technology of turning these data into smart tools to solve complex problems is becoming increasingly advanced, as computer systems evolve with increasing amounts of data to collect and compare, increasingly faster and better computers, and the greater amount of data required for research and testing.
